title: Sen. Tim Schaffer voted Yea on HB3, a school bus safety bill
text:
Sen. Tim Schaffer voted Yea on HB3, a school bus safety bill
Sen. Tim Schaffer (R-20th) voted Yea on HB3, a school bus safety bill, which passed the Ohio Senate 31-2 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill creates an August “School Bus Safety Awareness Month,” establishes a School Bus Safety Fund, and directs $25 million in each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027, plus related fines, to grants that help schools add or upgrade defined safety features on buses and support public education on bus laws. It strengthens penalties for illegally passing a stopped school bus, including higher fines, mandatory court appearances, license suspensions, possible safety-course requirements and adjusted license points, and requires notice of these rules when plates and licenses are issued. The bill also regulates use of school bus cameras, clarifies investigation procedures for reported violations, and slightly expands allowable small-capacity vehicles for pupil transportation.
HB3 was introduced by Rep. Bernard Willis and Rep. Cecil Thomas.
Schaffer is currently serving his fourth term in the Ohio Senate representing the 20th district, after being elected to the Ohio House in 2000 and later returning to the House in 2015.
He holds a Bachelor's degree in Political Science and Communications from Mount Union College and has held various leadership roles in several standing committees, including serving as Chairman of the Senate's Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee.
Schaffer has a history of addressing government corruption, reducing taxes, and supporting economic development initiatives that have led to job retention and creation in his districts.
His legislative contributions have earned him numerous accolades, including multiple Legislator of the Year awards from various organizations.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
